title: Indian-American Conservatives Face Racial Gatekeeping From the MAGA Fringe
excerpt: A Times of India report and U.S. coverage document racially charged attacks on Indian-American conservatives — from Ramaswamy's Ohio bid to Nikki Haley and JD Vance's family — even as immigration enforcement tightens around the community.
body:
• A Times of India report and U.S. press coverage document a run of racially charged attacks on prominent Indian-American conservatives — Vivek Ramaswamy, Nikki Haley, Trump Justice Department official Harmeet Dhillon and Vice President JD Vance's wife Usha — coming from the MAGA movement's fringes.
  • Ramaswamy, endorsed by President Trump and the Ohio Republican Party, has endured slurs, a "cowboys versus Indians" taunt from a primary rival and calls to "deport" him to India, a country where he has never lived. In January he stopped posting personally on X and Instagram.
  • The pattern is bipartisan in its targets: Democratic Representative Pramila Jayapal has faced "go back to India" abuse and death threats, while Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi rebuffed a "take your curry and go home" taunt this month.
  • The backdrop is tighter enforcement: 1,076 Indian nationals deported so far in 2026, per India's Ministry of External Affairs, and a reported review of up to 200,000 visitor visas that includes some 70,000 Indians.

For years, Indian-origin conservatives in Donald Trump's orbit told themselves that ideology, not ancestry, was the price of admission to the MAGA movement. A Times of India report suggests they are discovering an unwelcome asterisk: pass the ideological exam and still fail what the paper's Washington correspondent calls "the race test and dinner evaluation."

Incidents stack up on the right

Harmeet Dhillon, the Chandigarh-born lawyer leading the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division under Trump, was mocked by MAGA trolls after posting a photo of a beef dinner. Conservative commentator Dinesh D'Souza, defending his daughter from racist attacks, noted her mother is white — drawing ridicule.

Nikki Haley faced an earlier version: during her 2023 campaign, Ann Coulter told Haley — born in South Carolina to Sikh immigrants — to "go back to your own country," while Trump mocked her birth name, Nimarata, during the 2024 primary.

The pattern reached the vice president's family. After JD Vance became Trump's running mate in 2024, white-nationalist Nick Fuentes and others attacked his marriage to Usha Vance, who is of Indian ancestry, invoking "replacement" rhetoric. Vance told continuing critics to "eat s---."

Ramaswamy's campaign becomes the sharpest case

His Republican primary rival Casey Putsch posted an April video firing a rifle and inviting Ramaswamy to play "cowboys versus Indians" — "Don't worry. It's feather, not dot" — a slur distinguishing Indigenous people from people of Indian descent, the Columbus Dispatch reported. Putsch has also called Ramaswamy an "Indian, foreign national-born anchor baby billionaire."

"My social media feeds are littered with hundreds of slurs, most from accounts that I don't recognize, about 'pajeets' ... and calls to deport me 'back to India' (I was born and raised in Cincinnati and have never resided outside the U.S.)"

— Vivek Ramaswamy, in a December 2025 New York Times opinion piece

Ramaswamy, who built his career arguing race should not define American identity, now tells his own movement that "heritage Americans" have no superior claim to the country. In January, after his feeds filled with racist abuse, he quit personal posting on X and Instagram, writing in the Wall Street Journal that "leaders who depend on social media to gauge public opinion are looking through a broken mirror."

The enforcement backdrop

India's Ministry of External Affairs says 1,076 Indian nationals were deported from the U.S. so far in 2026, down from 3,567 in 2025, Livemint reported. The administration is also preparing to review up to 200,000 business and tourist visas held by people who later sought asylum — about 70,000 Indians reportedly included — in what would be the largest mass visa cancellation in U.S. history, per VisaVerge. This month a federal judge blocked a Trump rule replacing "duration of status" with fixed stays for foreign students, a population Indians dominate.

Bipartisan targets

Representative Pramila Jayapal, a Washington Democrat, has heard "go back to India" from MAGA extremists for years and faced death threats, including a man carrying a loaded Glock outside her Seattle home. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi was told this month to "take your curry and go home" — and answered publicly.

"I'm staying. So is the curry. America is my home. No bigot gets to decide who is American, who belongs here, or what they have for dinner. That's the America I'll always fight for."

— Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi

What to watch

The immediate test is Ohio's Republican primary, where Ramaswamy — backed by Trump, Governor Mike DeWine and the state party — remains the heavy favorite. Beyond Ohio, the open question is whether the Republican establishment treats racial attacks on its own candidates as a line worth defending — or as background noise of the online right. For Indian-Americans across party lines, political alignment has not bought immunity from American nativism's oldest question.
image_caption: The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. Indian-American conservatives say they face racial gatekeeping from parts of the MAGA movement.
nri_angle: Indian-Americans across party lines are learning that political alignment does not shield them from racial gatekeeping — while immigration enforcement tightens around the community.
author: Diaspora Desk
